title: Georgism Does Not Work The Way Its Advocates Believe (og/social title: "Georgist Taxes Are Paid By Renters, Not Landlords"; subtitle "Tax incidence, yay") — Doctor Hammer, Doc Hammer's Anvil (Substack), 26 September 2026, with comment thread to 29 September 2026

Fetched with curl and a browser user-agent (HTTP 200); body parsed from the page's embedded JSON; comments via the Substack API (https://dochammer.substack.com/api/v1/post/217414169/comments, post id 217414169, HTTP 200). Also fetched Scott Alexander's ACX host page for Doucet's 'Five Years Later' (HTTP 200) to read the four questions Hammer answers in context. The publication's /about page gave only a tagline. Saved under scratchpad t0-2026-10-10: hammer.html, hammer.txt, hammer_comments.json, hammer_comments.txt, acx_five_years.txt. NOT fetched: Hammer's earlier posts; Doucet's original 2021 Part 2.
verdict: ENRICH benefits/landlords-cannot-pass-lvt-to-tenants.md (no objections/ page on rent pass-through exists; the benefit page already carries a 'Short-run frictions are real' caveat bullet and is the home for it). Specific edits: (1) extend that bullet with a Tier 1-anchored sentence on adjustment speed (see content_summary 'Tier 1 anchor'); (2) add a two-sentence 'Current debate' note, clearly labelled, recording the exchange as origin-of-objection / origin-of-reply only. Optional one-sentence cross-note in research/doucet-does-georgism-work.md 'Five Years Later (2026)' (inbound from the benefit page already exists). Do NOT create a NEW objections page on the strength of this exchange; if the editor later wants a standalone objection ('A tax on land is a cost of housing and so passes to renters'), it should be built on Tier 1 sources (Löffler & Siegloch, Tsoodle & Turner, Nielsson et al., Mieszkowski/Zodrow) and cite Hammer at most as a popular statement of it.
claim_grade: D (argumentative/interpretive) — source tier under §4c: Doctor Hammer is pseudonymous with no stated or verifiable credentials, so Tier 3 on the §4c rubric (anonymous/pseudonymous source: subject of a page or own statements only), and at most a named Tier 2 'origin of the objection' if a blogger-level label is applied; never support. Lars Doucet is Tier 2 on sources/audit/people-tiers.json: origin of the reply only. Neither may be cited as evidence on incidence; the Tier 1 literature below carries the evidential weight.

content_summary.framing: Post is a response to Doucet's 'Does Georgism Work? Five Years Later' (ACX guest post, 24 Sept 2026; the wiki carries it at research/doucet-does-georgism-work.md). Hammer takes up the four questions Doucet said would change his mind (quoted in the post's opening section). Subtitle/description: 'Tax incidence, yay (a response to ACX)'. Footnote 2: 'the incidence of a land value tax is not the primary reason I think it is a bad idea.' Credentials: none stated; publication tagline 'Shaping Ideas on Life Economics, and Sometimes Metal'; author bio 'Probably not a supervillain building an army of robots in my basement... mad social science just doesn't get the grant money.' Footnote 7 jokes about defending 'your dissertation' but no degree or affiliation is claimed. Self-description in comments: lives near Philadelphia.
content_summary.scope_problem: Hammer's examples throughout are conventional property taxes ('a change in property tax from 3% to 0%', section 1c) and ordinary excise or sales taxes, and his conclusion treats a tax on land as a cost of 'providing housing'. He does not separate land from buildings until the comment thread. Doucet had already conceded in the post under reply that taxes on buildings do get passed on ('taxes on buildings do get passed on', Doucet comment 29 Sept) and that conventional-property-tax results are mixed.

mechanisms.claim: Rents fall slowly or not at all when landlord costs fall, but rise promptly when a cost hits all landlords at once. Hence the absence of downward adjustment is not evidence that tax increases are not passed on. Section 1: 'The short answer is that they do, but it takes a long time and is often swamped by other factors, so that on net the changes are not obvious.'
mechanisms.incidence_claim: Tax rises are passed to tenants 'as new leases get signed and old leases get renewed' (1f); price decreases are 'less common' and unnoticed by renters (1e).

mechanisms.claim: Cost-cutting landlords cannot expand output at low marginal cost: 'supply is short term very inelastic upwards for firms', so competition does not push rents down when costs fall. Taking units off the market is cheaper than adding units, so supply is 'sticky upwards'. Footnote 5 reports 5-10 years from starting a project to selling in the author's contractor brother-in-law's area.
mechanisms.incidence_claim: Because supply cannot expand quickly, a cost increase applying to all landlords is passed to renters (4a: 'the tax incidence will land nearly entirely on the consumer').

mechanisms.mechanism: 3. Contract rent lies between reservation prices; negotiation practice (1b, 1c, footnote 6)
mechanisms.claim: Agreed rent is almost never the tenant's maximum or the landlord's minimum; most Americans do not haggle ('the seller says "Rent is $2000 a month" and the buyer says "Ok."'). A 5% cost fall is not passed on because the tenant already agreed; a 5% rise is asked for and usually accepted. Small cost changes are small relative to rent and apartments are differentiated (1c). Footnote 6: at renewal a good tenant 'can negotiate either a decrease in rent or avoid an increase'.
mechanisms.incidence_claim: Landlords have the bargaining advantage on upward changes; tenants are 'less sensitive to price changes due to high cost of moving' (1d) and have little information on costs (1e).

mechanisms.claim: Leases are long and infrequently negotiated; a new tax is an industry-wide cost and a Schelling point, so landlords coordinate on it (2a), whereas they cannot coordinate a rent rise ahead of the tax. 1f: price increase 'will only take effect as new leases get signed and old leases get renewed, so the fastest the price difference can be measured is over the course of a year' (footnote 7: or the modal lease period).
mechanisms.incidence_claim: Answer to Doucet's question 2 (why not raise rents now?): coordination problem; no Schelling point until the tax is enacted.

answers_to_doucet_four_questions.Q3_developers_subtract_holding_costs_in_: 'Because that is how accounting rules work' (3a); Hammer says he is 'honestly not certain I understand the question'. He does not engage the capitalization point.
answers_to_doucet_four_questions.Q4_abolish_all_property_taxes: Yes, rents fall 'given enough time', though house prices 'might not' where supply is constrained (4a, and comment 28 Sept: 'Home buying works a bit more like auctions').

comments_verbatim_key_exchange.doucet_28_sept_05_20_UTC_two_cruxes: '1. You *don't* in fact think that landlords are currently charging as much as the market will bear? That in fact, they could charge much more, but various frictions are preventing them from doing so, and so ... they will therefore be able to increase the rent in response to an LVT being levied? 2. You do think, generally speaking, that if property taxes were suddenly abolished, rents and prices would indeed fall? If so, I applaud you for committing yourself to a testable hypothesis. My next question: what evidence could possibly get you to change your mind on the subject?' (comment id 347593390; quoted in full here because it is the two cruxes plus the falsifiability ask; about 90 words, so the T1 editor should quote only the cruxes' substance or a trimmed clause under the 50-word rule).
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.hammer_28_sept_reply: Crux 1: 'No, that's not what I am claiming ... I think landlords are charging roughly what the market will bear, but imposing a new broad tax changes the market, so the prices it will bear change.' Crux 2: yes, all else equal, a tax removal lowers the price; but 'all else equal does a good bit of work'. Evidence that would change his mind: 'you would need to show that renters are extremely sensitive to price' such that a large share would leave the area over a small rent rise, or that landlords would not change quantity or quality. He also asserts that 'excess' ground-rent profits 'have already been competed away'.
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.doucet_29_sept_00_20: Reframes crux as how the supply curve shifts. 'Tariffs are charged for every unit sold. However, an LVT is charged regardless of what the owner does with the land ... Which landlord decision is specifically changed by introducing an LVT?' Cites Wealth of Nations V.ii (quoted in the comment: 'A tax upon ground-rents would not raise the rents of houses').
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.hammer_29_sept_reply: Says the tax is a cost of 'using the land for anything' for all landlords, so the supply curve shifts up ('basic supply and demand analysis'); argues Smith's 'ground-rent' means money paid to a separate landowner and that where one person owns land and building 'ground-rents are zero'; cites Smith V.ii.e.4-5 on taxes on house-rent in general, which divide between tenant and ground-owner.
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.doucet_29_sept_03_26_two_follow_up_quest: '1. If ground rent is zero whenever the same person owns both the land and the building, what land value would an LVT tax, and what would there be to pass on to tenants? Empty lots in expensive cities sell for a lot of money ... 2. When a landlord sells, the buyer takes on the tax. Would a prospective buyer pay the same price for a particular piece of land after an LVT as before it?' He also notes Smith (V.ii.e.3, e.8, e.9) defines ground-rent as the price of 'some real or supposed advantage of the situation' and treats a tax on ground-rent alone as falling 'altogether upon the owner of the ground-rent'.
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.hammer_29_sept_04_07_and_04_42: Concedes the land price would be lower after an LVT ('as a matter of net present value. What's your point?'); argues a land price can fall with no ground-rent via a car-with-blue-paint analogy; says 'we don't sell land separately from the buildings here'; maintains that the landlord's business 'runs on net revenue, not the current value of the particular assets that were bought previously'.
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.doucet_29_sept_04_19_closing: 'if the price of land falls by the present value of the tax, then the owner has borne it, and the next person who buys it earns a normal return at the lower price without needing to raise rents ... taxes on buildings do get passed on (I happily conceded this in my original article), and rental markets do have real frictions ... I seem to have found [the crux]: whether a tax on land alone ends up in land prices or in rents.'
comments_verbatim_key_exchange.other_commenters: Jon Stokes, 'Incentives Matter' and Gustavo Zambrano praise the post; no substantive third-party economics. No academic economist engages in the thread.

content_summary.doucet_falsifiable_evidence_ask: Doucet asks, in his first reply, 'what evidence could possibly get you to change your mind'. Hammer's stated falsifier is large out-migration of renters from the taxed area (and quantity/quality response), which is a test of demand elasticity at the level of the whole taxed jurisdiction. Doucet's own implicit test is whether the land price falls by the present value of the tax. The thread ends with the cruxes identified but no agreed test; the wiki can note that the dispute reduces to 'tax on land alone: land price or rent?', which is exactly what the Danish, German and Norwegian capitalization studies on the wiki measure.

consistent_short_run: Rents adjust slowly and asymmetrically: Genesove (2003, Review of Economics and Statistics 85(4): 844-853) finds 29% of US apartment units had no nominal rent change year to year (1974-81 data), more where the same tenant stays, with downward resistance to rent cuts. Gallin & Verbrugge (2019, Journal of Economic Theory 183: 478-519) derive sticky rents from search and bargaining under incomplete information, with tenant moving costs exploited by multi-unit landlords. These support Hammer's mechanisms 1, 3 and 4 as descriptions of timing, in either direction.

Pass-through to rents of a combined land-plus-building property tax is gradual: Löffler & Siegloch (wiki page) find roughly a third of the burden in rents within two years and about 83% (2024 revision; 'full' in the 2021 version) after three, and lower pass-through where housing supply is inelastic.

Existing leases are fixed-term contracts, so any rent change (up or down) shows up only at renewal; this is ordinary and Doucet's own benefit-page caveat already says 'in the short run individual landlords may attempt pass-through in tight markets'.
Short-run housing supply is inelastic (Hammer 1a), which Hilber & Vermeulen (2016, Economic Journal; on wiki) and Hilber (2017, Real Estate Economics; on wiki) support for England/US generally.
not_consistent_with_mainstream_theory: Inference from short-run supply inelasticity to pass-through: standard incidence theory runs the other way. The less elastic the supply, the more of a tax falls on the supplier (Hammer's own comment of 28 Sept states this rule: 'if consumers can quit the market easily ... suppliers tend to pay the bill'). Inelastic supply of housing in the short run therefore points to owner incidence, not tenant incidence (Hilber 2017 on wiki: capitalization onto owners is 'more pronounced in locations with strict regulatory and geographical supply constraints').

Treating a tax assessed on land value as a 'cost of providing housing' that shifts the supply curve: the standard result (Mieszkowski 1972 'new view'; Zodrow 2001 'three views'; Mirrlees Review ch. 16; both on wiki) is that the land component of a property tax is a tax on a fixed factor, falls on the landowner, and is capitalized into land price. A tax independent of any decision of the landowner is a fixed cost, not a marginal cost, and does not shift marginal-cost supply.

Reading Adam Smith as implying 'ground-rents are zero' where one person owns land and building: Smith (WN V.ii.e, text at sources/publicdomain/wealth-of-nations.md) defines the surplus rent over builder's profit as ground-rent 'whatever part of the whole rent of a house is over and above what is sufficient for affording this reasonable profit naturally goes to the ground-rent' and says it is 'completely paid to the former' only 'where the owner of the ground and the owner of the building are two different persons'; the existence of the surplus does not depend on who owns it. Smith separately states 'A tax upon ground-rents would not raise the rent of houses'.

Denying capitalization: Hammer concedes the land price would fall by the NPV of the tax (comment 29 Sept), which is the owner-incidence result (Palmon & Smith, Oates 1969, Borge & Rattso, DOERS 2018, all on wiki). His 'blue paint' analogy concedes the point it was meant to resist.

Asserting 'tenants can't just live out of their cars' as an elasticity argument is a claim about demand elasticity in the aggregate; it supports pass-through only if housing supply is also elastic, the opposite of his premise 1a.
which_hammer_claims_are_consistent_with_.net_assessment: Hammer's frictions describe the TIMING of rent adjustments and are largely corroborated by Tier 1 work on rent rigidity; they do not alter the incidence of a tax on land alone, and several of his incidence inferences reverse the standard rule. The strongest legitimate residue is (a) building-inclusive property taxes can pass through (Löffler & Siegloch; Tsoodle & Turner; both on wiki), and (b) the Danish quasi-experiment (Nielsson, Wroblewski & Yding 2024, on wiki) finds a precise zero price effect and reads incidence as shared with tenants, which is a Tier 1 working paper making a stronger version of the opposing claim than Hammer does.

content_summary.tier1_anchor_literature: Standard result: Mirrlees Review ch. 16 (Tax by Design, 2011, pp. 368-405; on wiki: research/mirrlees-review.md), Mieszkowski (1972) and Zodrow (2001) (on wiki), Oates (1969) and Hamilton (1975/1976) (on wiki as research/oates-1969-capitalization.md and research/hamilton-benefit-tax.md). German pass-through: Löffler & Siegloch (on wiki), plus Buettner (2003, German land-tax capitalization with no rent effect; on wiki). Danish/Nordic: DOERS 2018 and Nielsson et al. 2024 (on wiki); Borge & Rattso 2014 (Norway; on wiki); Finland: Falkenbach, Harjunen, Makela & Oikarinen (2026) on Helsinki land-lease repricing (on wiki; shows capitalization of a ground-rent increase was 'real, but slow and uneven', which is the wiki's best Finnish illustration that adjustment can be slow without the burden shifting to tenants) and Lyytikainen (2009, Finnish three-rate property tax; on wiki). NOT on the wiki and recommended to add as Sources for any short-run-friction sentence: Genesove (2003) NBER w7137 / REStat; Gallin & Verbrugge (2019) JET and Cleveland Fed WP 17-05. Not located on the wiki: any study of commercial or residential lease-renewal timing specific to a land tax; Rolheiser's MIT work is mentioned on the Löffler & Siegloch page.
content_summary.suggested_wording_for_T1_editor: Benefit page, in the 'Short-run frictions are real' bullet: 'Rents adjust slowly: US apartment rents show substantial nominal rigidity, especially for continuing tenants (Genesove 2003), and search-and-bargaining models generate sticky rents without menu costs (Gallin & Verbrugge 2019); German property-tax increases reach rents gradually, about a third within two years (Löffler & Siegloch). Slow adjustment concerns timing and does not by itself change who bears a tax on a factor in fixed supply.' Then, in a 'Current debate' sub-paragraph: 'In September 2026 the pseudonymous Substack writer Doctor Hammer argued that rent stickiness, slow housing supply and lease-renewal timing mean land-based taxes reach tenants; the practitioner-author Lars Doucet replied in the comments that the dispute turns on whether a tax on land alone falls on land prices or on rents. Both are cited as the origin of each position, not as evidence.' (No grade codes or access notes in prose per §4b.)

existing_wiki_coverage: benefits/landlords-cannot-pass-lvt-to-tenants.md (46 inbound) already carries: the building-versus-land distinction ('evidence about the property tax sets a ceiling'), Löffler & Siegloch, Tsoodle & Turner, Nielsson et al., Feldstein as challenged_by, Hilber (2017) supply-elasticity conditional, and a 'Short-run frictions are real' bullet ('individual landlords may attempt pass-through in tight markets'); supported_by lists doucet-does-georgism-work. last_reviewed 2026-07-18, so it predates the Five Years Later piece and Hammer. research/doucet-does-georgism-work.md has a 'Five Years Later (2026)' section recording Doucet's Danish rent-control exception and listing his tests ('why landlords don't cut rents when their costs fall; why property developers still discount land-tax holding costs into offering prices'), but does not record any reply. Neither Hammer nor the exchange appears on the wiki. No objections/ page addresses rent pass-through (closest: objections/lvt-is-just-a-property-tax.md, which links Löffler & Siegloch and Hamilton as 'incidence results for a combined land-and-building tax cannot be read across'; and objections/lvt-transition-wealth-shock.md, which carries Nielsson et al.). Genesove (2003) and Gallin & Verbrugge are not on the wiki (grep of all .md files finds neither). research/tourek-drc-progressive-property-tax.md (read as instructed) is a DRC progressivity field experiment and has no bearing on this item.
uncertainties: Hammer argues that landlords have a cheap exit (sell, convert to commercial, mothball) while tenants do not, i.e. that supply is elastic on the downside; that is an empirical premise (and a long-run one) which sits uneasily with his own premise that supply is inelastic on the upside. The T1 editor should present this as his stated reasoning rather than as a settled contradiction.

Several verbatim comment quotations in content_summary exceed 50 words (Doucet 28 Sept; Doucet 29 Sept 03:26); they are recorded for the editor's reading and must be trimmed or paraphrased for the page.
Hammer's identity and credentials are unknowable from the page; 'Doctor' may be a pen-name rather than a degree. The wiki should not describe him as an economist.

Substack timestamps are UTC; 'Doucet replies in the comments (28 September)' is accurate for the first reply (05:20 UTC 28 Sept); the exchange runs to 04:43 UTC 29 Sept. Doucet's ACX guest post is dated 24 September on the existing wiki page.
The og/social title ('Georgist Taxes Are Paid By Renters, Not Landlords') differs from the page headline ('Georgism Does Not Work The Way Its Advocates Believe'); cite the headline plus URL.

The Genesove and Gallin & Verbrugge abstracts were read via search-result abstracts (NBER w7137 page, IDEAS/RePEc), not the full papers; the T1 editor should open NBER w7137 and the IDEAS record before citing figures.
I did not read Mirrlees ch. 16 afresh; the wiki's own page records the 'almost undeniable' quote as verified against the IFS PDF.

I did not locate a Tier 1 paper that directly tests rent adjustment to a pure land-value-tax rate change at lease renewal; Buettner (2003) and DOERS (2018) are the closest and the DOERS paper infers the no-pass-through result from capitalization rather than a Danish rent regression.

title: From Ground Rent to Compute Rent — Jiayi Jessica Ye & Yanmei Lin, Vermont Law Review blog (VLR Blog), posted 9 October 2026 (page byline: 'Written by Tech Editor')
what_was_fetched: Full post text and all 25 footnotes, read in full (curl with browser user-agent, HTTP 200). Saved as ye.html / ye.txt. The page carries no author biographies. Yanmei Lin's faculty profile fetched through r.jina.ai (the vermontlaw.edu page returns a Cloudflare block to curl; HTTP 403, then reachable by the r.jina.ai step of the ladder). No source for Jiayi Jessica Ye located: the Vermont Law Review author-search and tag pages show only the post, and web searches of Vermont Law's directory found no matching person. None of the post's cited sources were opened (footnote claims below are as the authors state them).
verdict: REJECT. Not worth an attributed sentence in concepts/taxing-tech-rents.md §6 or on a Paine page at this time. Reasons: (1) it is a short student-edited law-review blog post (about 1,500 words), not peer-reviewed scholarship, by an unverifiable co-author and a Vermont Law professor of environmental/China law writing outside her field, which on §4c is Tier 2 at best (origin of a coinage only); (2) 'compute rent' is a one-off coinage with no uptake that this wiki can show, and it is a misnomer: the instrument proposed is a data dividend or licensing levy on training data funding a UBI, not a rent on compute (taxing-tech-rents.md §6 is about compute, token and robot taxes, so inserting it would blur §6 with §4 'Data Dividends / Data-as-Labor'); (3) the wiki already covers every strand with Tier 1 sources: Paine and the ground-rent/citizen's-dividend lineage (people/thomas-paine.md, texts/agrarian-justice.md, concepts/citizens-dividend.md), data-as-labor (Arrieta-Ibarra et al.), Korinek & Stiglitz, Korinek & Lockwood, IMF SDN 2024/001; (4) the post misstates its own cited figures (see content_summary). If the editor nevertheless wants to record the phrase, the least-bad single sentence would go in concepts/data-as-labor.md (not §6) as 'a 2026 student-edited law-review blog post coins 'compute rent' for a data dividend funded by AI developers and paid as a UBI', attributed and unsupported; but REJECT is the recommendation.
claim_grade: D (argumentative/normative) — source tier under §4c: Tier 2 at best, 'origin of a term only, never support'. Lin is a recognised scholar of comparative environmental law at Vermont Law and Graduate School but not on taxation, AI or property theory; Ye's status is unverified; the venue is a student-edited review's blog. The post cites no empirical evidence of its own.

content_summary.authors_and_affiliation: Page names 'Jiayi Jessica Ye, Yanmei Lin' with no affiliations. Yanmei Lin (vermontlaw.edu/faculty/lin-yanmei, read via r.jina.ai): Professor of Law and Director, U.S.-Asia Partnerships for Environmental Law, Vermont Law and Graduate School; PhD China University of Political Science and Law, LLM NYU; over 40 articles in comparative environmental law (public-interest litigation, wildlife, access and benefit sharing of genetic resources); 2022 Richard Brooks Distinguished Faculty Scholar. Jiayi Jessica Ye: not located on the school's directory pages reachable; likely a student or fellow of the school's Asia programme, but that is an inference and not evidenced. The Vermont Law Review describes itself as 'a quarterly student-edited legal journal'.
argument_structure: 1. Frame: AI value derives from a shared 'digital commons' (prompts, Wikipedia edits, public web), yet flows to a few firms; usually framed as copyright/licensing/regulation.

2. Paine: Agrarian Justice (1797) grounds a rights-based theory: improvement cannot be separated from the earth, so the landowner owes society 'ground rent' for enclosing the common inheritance. Cited quotation: Paine, 'It is impossible to separate the improvement made by cultivation from the earth itself' (fn 3, ssa.gov copy).

3. Extension: 'If ground-rent is the price paid for enclosing common land, compute-rent is the price AI developers should pay for enclosing the digital commons that makes their models.' LLMs without human data are 'hollow shells'; Microsoft, Google and Meta are 'de facto digital landlords' (fn 5, a Journal d'un Progressiste post).

4. Non-rivalry objection (see below), then innovation-incentive objection answered in one sentence: Paine 'doesn't deny returns on improvement. It only insists that improvement don't erase the commons that made it possible.'

5. Why not market or state mechanisms: contributors cannot bargain collectively; developers have no incentive to pay; governments 'hoard the money'. Litigation (NYT v. Microsoft) and licensing (Reddit) compensate rights-holders and platforms, not contributors.

6. Remedy: a public trust holds 'compute-rent' and disburses it universally by right, i.e. UBI as restitution, financed by a 'data dividend' via 'taxes on excess profits or licensing fees on public data trained models'. Universality justified by the attribution problem.
7. Legitimacy argument (Paine): perceived injustice makes property fragile; UBI stabilises property. Conclusion: 'twenty-first-century AI developers owe compute-rent.'
content_summary.non_rivalry_handling: Concedes the objection directly, citing Shapiro & Varian, Information Rules (1999): 'information doesn't deplete when used' and 'there's no exclusion in the way there was during the Enclosure Acts.' Reply: 'while data is non-rivalrous, the economic opportunity derived from it is rivalrous. If an LLM can simulate a writer's style, it occupies the market spots previously held by humans.' This is a substitution-in-the-output-market argument, not an argument that data is rivalrous; no engagement with the non-excludability of the commons or with the valuation problem the wiki records on taxing-tech-rents.md §4.
figures_and_named_sources: 'about 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies are at risk due to AI' — attributed to the IMF, fn 9: Cazzaniga et al., Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work, IMF SDN/2024/001. MISSTATED: the IMF note (wiki: research/imf-gen-ai-future-of-work.md, read in full) says 60% of advanced-economy jobs are 'exposed' to AI, with roughly half of exposed jobs facing potential complementarity (augmentation) and half displacement risk; it is not a count of jobs 'at risk'.

'by 2030, as many as 375 million workers across the globe will face job disruption and need to switch occupations' — fn 10: Manyika et al., Jobs Lost, Jobs Gained, McKinsey Global Institute (2017). Placed in the sentence after the IMF figure so that a reader may attribute it to the IMF; it is a 2017 automation scenario figure (fastest-adoption scenario) not an AI-specific forecast. Not checked at source.

'In 2025, the five largest firms, OpenAI, Anthropic, NVIDIA, Adobe and Microsoft, together held roughly 50 percent of the market' — fn 6: MarketsandMarkets (a commercial market-research vendor page). Not checked; low-grade source.
'OpenAI and Google pay Reddit about $130 million per year combined' — fns 18-19: Reuters (Feb 2024) and Adweek (Feb 2025). The $130 million is the authors' sum; not checked.

'GPT-4 was trained on trillions of data drawn from public web and academic archives' — fn 4: Luo et al., Scientific Reports 15: 14119 (2025), a Chinese medical-licensing-exam evaluation paper, an odd citation for training-data scale.

Korinek: fn 23, Korinek, Schindler & Stiglitz, 'Technological Progress and Artificial Intelligence', in How to Achieve Inclusive Growth (OUP, 2021), cited for 'because AI creates massive economic rents for information monopolies, failing to redistribute these gains will lead to severe societal friction'. This is a different work from the Korinek & Stiglitz (2017) NBER paper on the wiki (research/korinek-stiglitz-ai-rents.md). Not opened; the paraphrase of the chapter is the authors'. Fn 24 Acemoglu & Restrepo (JEP 2019); fn 12 Verdegem (AI & Society 2024); fn 15 Vertesi et al. (FAccT 2026) support the social-unrest and commons points. No tax-incidence, elasticity or revenue figures are given anywhere.
content_summary.assessment_of_phrase: 'Compute rent' (also written 'compute-rent') appears nowhere on the wiki outside sources/wiki-queue.json (this queue entry). The authors introduce it hedged ('what might be called compute-rent') and use it to mean compensation for enclosing the digital commons through a data dividend; it is not a Georgist rent-on-compute concept, and the wiki's rent analysis (law-of-rent, taxing-tech-rents) treats compute as an input where the Korinek & Lockwood warning applies ('taxes on compute or robot ownership are capital taxes'). Its closest relatives on the wiki are the data-dividend / data-as-labor family (C-minus on taxing-tech-rents.md §4) and the citizen's dividend. Tier 2 origin credit is available but not warranted by notability: no uptake, no scholarly venue.

existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/taxing-tech-rents.md: §4 'Data Dividends / Data-as-Labor — C-minus' (Arrieta-Ibarra, Goff, Jimenez-Hernandez, Lanier & Weyl 2018; Posner & Weyl; valuation problem named: 'no one has a working method to price an individual's non-rival data contribution'); §6 'AI-Specific Taxes — Compute, Token, and Robot Taxes — D (provisional)' (Korinek & Lockwood 2026 sort instruments by what they economically are; compute/ownership taxes are capital taxes); §7 public equity stakes; 'The AI Coda' (Korinek & Stiglitz 2017; Korinek & Vipra 2025; Korinek & Lockwood 2026). research/imf-gen-ai-future-of-work.md (read in full; explicit that exposure is not displacement and that it 'does not recommend a universal basic income, AI dividend, or sovereign-wealth-style mechanism'). concepts/data-as-labor.md, concepts/data-rents.md, concepts/citizens-dividend.md (Paine as Predecessor; Dramé brief linking AI/automation to a land-rent-funded dividend, flagged as advocacy). people/thomas-paine.md, texts/agrarian-justice.md (full public-domain text, 10 inbound), concepts/ground-rent.md, books/with-liberty-and-dividends-for-all.md. The phrase 'compute rent' is absent from all wiki pages. No page records a Paine-to-AI analogy.
uncertainties: Ye's affiliation could not be established; the 'student-edited' character of the post is inferred from the journal's self-description and the 'Written by Tech Editor' byline, not from an author note.
Footnoted figures were not traced to source; only the IMF misreading was checked (against the wiki's full-text page on the IMF note).
The Korinek-Schindler-Stiglitz 2021 chapter was not opened, so whether it supports the sentence it is cited for is unknown.

If the editor believes novelty of a Paine-to-AI extension merits mention, the more defensible Tier 1 home for the underlying idea is Korinek & Lockwood (2026) and Korinek & Stiglitz (2017) already on the wiki, not this post.

title: Appendix 7: Deadweight economic loss caused by raising revenue for projects and programs — Leo Dobes, Joanne Leung & George Argyrous, in Social Cost-Benefit Analysis in Australia and New Zealand: The State of Current Practice and What Needs to be Done (ANU Press, ANZSOG series, 2016; DOI 10.22459/SCBAANZ.04.2016), pp. 203-212
what_was_fetched: Full PDF downloaded (curl, browser user-agent, HTTP 200; 11 pages = book pp. 203-212 plus licence page) and parsed locally with pymupdf; all text, Boxes and Tables A7.1-A7.3 read in full (saved as app07.pdf, dobes_app07.txt). Primary follow-up: Treasury Working Paper 2015-01 (Cao et al.) downloaded in full from treasury.gov.au (77 pages, saved cao2015.pdf, cao2015.txt) to check the 'Cao et al. 2015' values. NOT obtained: KPMG Econtech (2010), 'CGE Analysis of the Current Australian Tax System' (Treasury, Henry Review input) — two guessed Treasury URLs returned 404 and a search did not surface the PDF; Table A7.2 values are therefore as reproduced by Dobes et al. from KPMG Econtech (2010, p. 5). ANU Press landing page and ANU research-portal record fetched (r.jina.ai); authors' institutional titles are not stated in the fetched pages.
verdict: ENRICH concepts/deadweight-loss.md (add a 'Practice' paragraph in 'The Excess Burden of the Current Tax System', replacing the uncited '20 to 50 cents' sentence), with a one-sentence secondary addition to places/australia.md. NEW is not warranted: the appendix is an eleven-page appendix of a public-policy handbook, the wiki has no cost-benefit-analysis cluster to hang a page on, and the two Tier 1 primaries (KPMG Econtech 2010; Cao et al. 2015) would be better ingested as research pages only if the editor wants an Australian excess-burden cluster (candidate: research/cao-et-al-treasury-marginal-excess-burden.md with inbound links from deadweight-loss, places/australia, research/tideman-avoidable-excess-burden).
claim_grade: B (empirical, secondary reporting of official-model estimates) for the tabulated METB values — Tier 1: Dobes and Argyrous and Leung are recognised public-policy / cost-benefit academics (ANU Press, which describes its books as fully peer-reviewed; Dobes is listed by ANZSOG as Honorary Associate Professor at the ANU Crawford School; Leung's and Argyrous's titles were not confirmed), and the underlying numbers come from Treasury-commissioned (KPMG Econtech) and Treasury-staff (Cao et al.) CGE modelling, official-body Tier 1. C for the authors' methodological critique ('rubbery', harmonisation), which is their own assessment.

content_summary.definitions: p. 203: raising revenue 'is itself not costless' because of collection and compliance costs and because revenue measures 'preclude activity or transactions that would otherwise have occurred, with consumer and producer surplus being forgone'. Box A7.1 (p. 204, from Bates 2001, pp. 50-51): the Jack-and-Jenny lawn-mowing example, a $5 surplus lost by a 30% tax. p. 205: 'marginal excess tax burden (METB)' is the deadweight loss divided by revenue collected; 'In the case of a tax with an METB of 1.30, for example, raising $1 in revenue would impose a cost of $1.30 on the economy.' Also p. 205: 'A land tax, for example, is often regarded as being relatively efficient because the low price elasticity of demand results in a relatively lower loss of consumer surplus' (their wording says demand elasticity; the standard argument is inelastic supply — flag if quoted). If land is mostly foreign-owned 'the loss of social surplus would be even lower' because foreigners lack standing in a national CBA. Textbooks advise adjusting project costs by (1 + METB) (Brown & Campbell 2003; Boardman et al. 2011) but 'this rarely occurs in practice'; Campbell & Brown (2003, p. 224) argue the marginal cost of tax revenue approximates the marginal cost of public funds from any source.
content_summary.table_A7_1_labour_supply_METB_studies: p. 207, compiled by Argyrous: Findlay & Jones (1982) Australia 23-65% (labour income); Diewert & Lawrence (1995) NZ 14-18%; Freebairn (1995) Australia 2.6-72.7% (labour income); Campbell & Bond (1997) Australia 19-24% (1988-89 data); Bates (2001) NZ 50%; KPMG Econtech (2010) Australia -8% to 92% (2008; Table A7.2); Cao et al. (2015) Australia -10% to 75% (2007-08 and 2013-14; company income, personal income, goods and services, land, stamp duty and conveyances). Defaults in use: NZ Treasury Cost Benefit Analysis Primer (2005, p. 18) 'a rate of 20% as a default deadweight loss value'; Australian Government Handbook of Cost-Benefit Analysis (Dept of Finance and Administration 2006, p. 37) 25% citing Campbell (1997); Victorian Dept of Treasury and Finance (2013, p. 51) default METB 1.08, 'on the basis that the government could finance its projects from the most efficient state tax source (i.e. land tax)' (p. 211). White et al. (2012) use 10% unexplained; Moore et al. (2010) defer to NZ Treasury's 20%.
content_summary.table_A7_2_plug_in_values: pp. 210-211, 'Marginal excess burdens of Australian taxes (cents of consumer welfare per dollar of revenue)', Source: KPMG Econtech (2010, p. 5): Tobacco excise -8; Import duties -3; Petroleum resource rent tax 0; Municipal rates 2; GST 8; Land taxes 8; Alcohol excise/WET 9; Fuel taxes 15; Stamp duties other than real property 18; Luxury car tax 20; Labour income tax 24; Conveyancing stamp duties 34; Motor vehicle registration 37; Motor vehicle stamp duties 38; Corporate income tax 40; Payroll tax 41; Insurance taxes 67; Royalties and crude oil excise 70; Gambling taxes 92. Land tax, stamp duty (conveyancing and other), payroll tax and company tax all appear with values. Highest are gambling (92), royalties/crude oil excise (70) and insurance (67); conveyancing stamp duty is 34 (sixth-highest tier of the 19 listed, not the highest). Land tax and municipal rates are the lowest positive values (8 and 2). Note: the brief's premise 'land tax near zero, stamp duty highest' fits Cao et al. (below) but NOT this KPMG table, where land tax is 8 and stamp duty on conveyances is 34.
content_summary.table_A7_3_state_taxes: p. 211, Gabbitas & Eldridge (1998, Productivity Commission), METB of state taxation in presence of Commonwealth taxation and externalities: leaded petrol 6, unleaded 4, diesel 4, tobacco 28, normal beer 14, low-alcohol beer 15, wine 12, spirits 58. No land tax, stamp duty or payroll tax values in this table. Dobes et al. note externality-adjusted values are lower, consistent with Boardman et al.
content_summary.albon_1997: Albon (1997) is cited once, on p. 203, as a review of 'a wide range of taxes imposed specifically by the states and territories'; the appendix reproduces NO Albon METB values. The brief's 'Albon 1997' plug-in source is not present in this appendix; the sources for tabulated values are KPMG Econtech (2010), Gabbitas & Eldridge (1998), Cao et al. (2015) and the labour-supply studies in A7.1.
content_summary.authors_critique: pp. 207-209: Campbell & Bond (1997, 19-24%) rests on 1988-89 data and on Apps & Savage (1989) labour supply parameters from 1981-82 for 'couple income units with a male head aged 25-54' (p. 208), so 'it seems inappropriate that the Commonwealth Treasury should uncritically adopt an METB of 25 per cent' and the estimate 'would benefit from updating and re-estimation'. Estimates are 'very sensitive to the estimation model and the parameter assumptions' (Freebairn 1995, p. 127, quoted p. 207). Many CBAs ignore METB, apply a labour-income METB where financing is by equity or user charges (the NBN CBA used 0.24, p. 209), or copy unexplained values. Changed labour markets (part-time, female participation, backward-bending supply for some groups, p. 210); CGE models assume full employment, whereas involuntary unemployment changes METB (Freebairn 1995; p. 212). pp. 212 'A7.4 Conclusion': 'Estimates of deadweight loss are fraught with assumptions and data issues.' Project-specific estimation would be 'prohibitive', so analysts use others' 'plug-in' values. 'Given the essentially 'rubbery' nature of estimates of deadweight loss, jurisdictions should consider a more harmonised approach' (p. 212).
content_summary.recommendations: p. 212, 'a more harmonised approach that includes': (i) the extent to which deadweight losses should be included in CBA; (ii) 'the desirability of agreement on deadweight loss factors for a number of the more common revenue-raising instruments'; (iii) 'an agreed approach for easy updating of METB estimates between periodic major reviews'. p. 209 issues for a harmonised value: labour-supply elasticities, income tax rates and distribution, and awareness of programme economic impact.
content_summary.cao_et_al_2015_primary_check: Cao, Hosking, Kouparitsas, Mullaly, Rimmer, Shi, Stark & Wende (the working paper's cover names Cao, Kouparitsas, Mullaly, Rimmer, Shi, Stark and Wende; IDEAS also lists Hosking), 'Understanding the economy-wide efficiency and incidence of major Australian taxes', Treasury Working Paper 2015-01 (April 2015). Read in full (abstract, Tables 2-6, sensitivity analysis). Baseline marginal excess burdens per dollar of net revenue: hypothetical broad-based land tax (municipal rates plus a broad land tax on investment property) -10 cents ('a result of the inclusion of the foreign ownership share of factor income from land', about 10% — domestic households gain from transferring income from foreign landowners; sensitivity range -0.20 to 0.00); stamp duty on conveyances +72 cents (sensitivity 0.10 to 1.15, 'largely determined by the elasticity of substitution in the structures and land bundle'); company income tax about +50 cents; flat labour income tax about 21 cents; GST about 19 cents (the paper notes KPMG 2010 had GST at 8 and KPMG 2011 at 12). Abstract: 'stamp duty on conveyances and the company income tax are the least efficient taxes ... while the most efficient tax is a hypothetical broad-based land tax'. Caveat in text (p. 51-52 of the paper): 'The current exemptions and concessions to land tax would raise the marginal excess burden from the highly efficient broad-based land tax modelled in this paper.' Incidence: the paper says an increase in broad-based land tax 'is completely borne by the land-owners'. Payroll tax is not modelled in Cao et al. (its taxes are company income, personal income, GST, land, stamp duty); payroll tax 41 appears only in the KPMG table. The appendix's range '-10% to 75%' for Cao et al. does not match the baseline 72 for stamp duty I found (75 may arise from another scenario in the paper; unresolved).
content_summary.relevance_to_wiki_claims: The existing wiki line 'Estimates of this excess burden typically range from 20 to 50 cents per dollar of revenue ... LVT is the one major revenue source with no excess burden' has no citation. Australian official modelling supports the ranking (land the most efficient, conveyancing stamp duty and company tax the least) but shows nuance the wiki should carry: the KPMG Econtech figure for actual Australian state land taxes is +8 cents (not zero), reflecting exemptions, thresholds and the foreign-ownership accounting; Cao et al.'s -10 is for a hypothetical broad-based land tax and is a foreign-ownership artefact rather than a negative deadweight loss on domestic owners. These are model outputs from a stylised representative-household CGE model, the authors of the appendix themselves call such numbers 'rubbery', and a Tier 1 reader will expect that stated.

suggested_sentences: concepts/deadweight-loss.md — 'Practice' paragraph in 'The Excess Burden of the Current Tax System' (replace the uncited '20 to 50 cents' sentence): 'Australian and New Zealand government cost-benefit practice treats the marginal excess burden of a tax (the deadweight loss per dollar of revenue) as a plug-in value, and a review of that practice finds the values rest on a few labour-supply studies and on computable-general-equilibrium work of limited vintage; New Zealand Treasury guidance defaults to 20 per cent, the Australian federal handbook to 25 per cent, and Victoria's Treasury to 8 per cent on the grounds that land tax is the state's most efficient revenue source (Dobes, Leung & Argyrous 2016, App. 7).'

concepts/deadweight-loss.md — same paragraph, second sentence: 'The widely used Australian ranking, from Treasury-commissioned modelling (KPMG Econtech 2010), puts land taxes at 8 cents of welfare cost per dollar of revenue and municipal rates at 2, against 34 for conveyancing stamp duties, 40 for company income tax and 41 for payroll tax; a later Treasury working paper (Cao et al. 2015) found a hypothetical broad-based land tax the most efficient of the taxes modelled, at minus 10 cents once foreign ownership of land is counted, and conveyancing stamp duty (72 cents) and company income tax (about 50 cents) the least. Its authors caution that existing exemptions would raise the land-tax figure, and the reviewers of this practice describe such estimates as "rubbery" and call for agreed, regularly updated values.'

places/australia.md — one sentence under 'What the Land Is Worth, and What a Land Tax Could Replace', after the substitution arithmetic: 'Treasury modelling of Australia's own taxes ranks land taxes and municipal rates as among the least costly sources of revenue per dollar raised and conveyancing stamp duty among the most costly (Cao et al. 2015; KPMG Econtech 2010, as tabulated in Dobes, Leung & Argyrous 2016), the ranking that underlies the Henry Review's preference for shifting from stamp duty to land tax.' (Last clause links only if the editor can source the Henry Review claim; the Henry Review final report is already cited as source 6 on places/australia.md.)

Sources annotation for each: 'Dobes, Leung & Argyrous (2016), ANU Press, App. 7, pp. 203-212 — used for the practice of plug-in METB values, Table A7.1-A7.3 and the harmonisation critique (B-claim; peer-reviewed press, Tier 1; Table A7.2 is a secondary reproduction of KPMG Econtech 2010, p. 5, whose full report was not accessible at last review (2026-10-10)).'
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/deadweight-loss.md (77 inbound): definition, why LVT has zero deadweight loss, Smith and Pigou antecedents, Gaffney's alternative measure, Gross & Klein's partial-equilibrium qualification; its 'Excess Burden of the Current Tax System' section states an uncited '20 to 50 cents per dollar of revenue' range and 'LVT is the one major revenue source with no excess burden'. No 'practice', cost-benefit-analysis or marginal-cost-of-public-funds content: grep for 'marginal excess', 'METB' and 'marginal cost of public funds' across all wiki .md files hits only research/tideman-avoidable-excess-burden.md (US dynamic CGE: MEB of five US taxes recovered as revenue shifts to land). Neither KPMG Econtech (2010) nor Cao et al. (2015) nor Dobes et al. appears anywhere on the wiki (grep of all .md and .json files). places/australia.md covers the 1910-52 federal land tax, state land taxes, Victoria's land-tax increases, the ABS substitution arithmetic ($34.4 bn conveyance duties, $20.0 bn land taxes, $25.1 bn rates), the Henry Review (source 6), AHURI stamp-duty study (source 7) and Creighton's IPA oration; it has no efficiency-cost estimate. places/new-zealand.md covers rates, the 2026 TOP proposal and the Inland Revenue LTIB incidence statement; no cost-benefit-analysis content. research/gross-klein-partial-equilibrium-welfare-market-power-taxes.md (read as instructed) is the closest conceptual neighbour: it shows the standard formula assumes all other markets are undistorted, which is also a reason the CGE METB values vary by model.
uncertainties: KPMG Econtech (2010) not obtained; Table A7.2 is therefore second-hand (via Dobes et al.), cross-checked only indirectly: Cao et al. cite KPMG (2010) GST at 8 cents, which matches the table's GST 8.

Dobes et al. give land tax 8 and municipal rates 2 as separate lines; Cao et al. combine them in one hypothetical tax. The two are not like-for-like and the wiki should not state a single 'Australian METB for land tax'.

Cao et al.'s negative value reflects 10% foreign ownership of land income in a national-standing welfare measure; it is not evidence that taxing land has negative deadweight loss for domestic owners, and quoting '-10 cents' without that caveat would mislead.
The appendix's Table A7.1 range for Cao et al. (-10% to 75%) does not match the 72 cents baseline I read for stamp duty; unresolved.

Affiliations of Dobes, Leung and Argyrous (ANU Crawford School; ANZSOG) were not confirmed from the fetched pages; ANZSOG's site lists Dobes as Honorary Associate Professor at the Crawford School. The book is in the ANZSOG series under ANU Press.
The Victorian default METB of 1.08 (Victorian Treasury and Finance 2013, p. 51) is as reported by Dobes et al.; the Victorian primary was not opened.
Appendix covers 2016 practice; Australian and NZ guidance may have changed since (the NZ Treasury CBAx tool and Australian Office of Impact Analysis guidance were not checked).
